title: Question about The Hunted (2003) and Del Toro's character

commenti.body:
I think The Hunted if a B-movie genre flick *seriously* elevated by Friedkin’s direction and Jones’ and Del Toro’s performances.

On paper, it’s ridiculous. But they sell the hell out of it and now I own it and I’ve seen it so many times. And that ambiguity that you mention is so important IMO. 

On the one hand, moments like “they’re robots” can easily be read as signs of mental problems, and it seems that Jones and them decide to read them that way. On the other, you’re right that the agents are played so creepy and unsavory that it’s easy to imagine they are some sort of black ops cleanup crew, arriving on the scene to eliminate the evidence. And then you end up being right. They’re blackbag killers. This lends to it also being forever unclear as to whether or not the guys in the beginning are hunters or another cleanup crew.

So is Hallam nuts or is he actually hunted? Honestly, I go for both. The government is trying to kill him and* Hallam has snapped. After all, he kills without remorse, continually, even regular cops who don’t really know shit about what’s happening. We know Hallam is haunted by nightmares, and now seems to have lost the ability to care about who it is he’s killing to accomplish his mission.

And, in the end, I think LT is the only person he trusts at all—a father figure of sorts—and the man who has to kill him. LT being forced to kill (as opposed to just teaching the theory) is him being confronted with the sins of his past and his role in all of this violence. Him burning the letters feels like denial searching for closure.

It's weird because from the beginning LT is very hostile towards Hallam (immediately fighting him when Hallam is trying to talk, pretending not to know who he is). Makes me feel more for Hallam who doesn't really do much wrong until killing that construction worker. I also recently watched the first couple of seasons of Dexter so the government agent they sent after him I was more suspicious of as he plays a manipulative character in that show

>How much of Hallam's (Belnicio Del Toro's character) mental degradation was legitimate?

100% of it.

Hallam is what would happen to someone like Jason Bourne in real life.

>My biggest problem was that Hallam tried to get help from LT and got nothing

This is a fair complaint. Veterans are treated like shit in this country. Really good article about a real life Aaron Hallam, here: https://harpers.org/archive/2024/01/matt-farwell-the-museum-of-broken-g-i-joes/

It is interesting, to me that LT kept Hallam's letters and feels guilty enough about his failure that he burns them.
